column2: And the Sun rose up, leaving the very beautiful lake,
into the brazen sky, to shine for the immortals
and for mortal men upon the grain-giving earth;
and they came to Pylos, the well-built citadel of Neleus.
And they were performing sacrifices on the shore of the sea,
all-black bulls, to the dark-haired Earth-shaker.
There were nine seats, and in each five hundred
sat, and in each they presented nine bulls.
When they had tasted the innards, and were burning thigh-pieces for the god,
these men steered straight in, and the sails of the balanced ship
they furled and lifted, and moored her, and themselves stepped out.
And Telemachus stepped out of the ship, and Athena led.
To him first spoke the goddess, grey-eyed Athena:
Then wise Telemachus answered her in turn:
Then again the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, said to him:

Telemachus, some things you yourself will think of in your own mind,
27	and others a god will suggest; for I do not think
28	that you were born and reared without the will of the gods.
So speaking, Pallas Athena led the way
swiftly; and he then followed in the footsteps of the goddess.
And they came to the gathering and seats of the Pylian men,
where Nestor sat with his sons, and around him companions
preparing the feast were roasting meat and putting other on spits.
And when they saw the strangers, they all came together,
and greeted them with their hands and bade them sit.
First Nestor's son Peisistratus, coming near,
took the hand of both and seated them at the feast
on soft fleeces on the sandy shore,
beside his brother Thrasymedes and his father;
and he gave them portions of the innards, and poured wine
into a golden cup; and pledging her he addressed
Pallas Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus:

Pray now, stranger, to lord Poseidon;
44	for it is his feast that you have chanced upon in coming here.
45	And when you have poured a libation and prayed, as is right,
46	give then to this man also the cup of honey-sweet wine
47	to pour a libation, since I think that he too prays
48	to the immortals; and all men have need of the gods.
49	But he is younger, and of the same age as I myself;
50	therefore to you first I shall give the golden goblet.
So saying he put in her hand the cup of sweet wine;
and Athena rejoiced at the wise and just man,
because he had given her first the golden goblet;
and at once she prayed much to lord Poseidon:

Hear me, Poseidon, earth-holder, and do not begrudge
56	us who pray that these deeds be accomplished.
57	To Nestor first of all and to his sons grant glory,
58	and then to the others give a gracious recompense
59	to all the Pylians for the glorious hecatomb;
60	and grant also that Telemachus and I, having accomplished it, return,
61	for which we came here with our swift black ship.
So then she prayed, and herself accomplished it all.
And she gave Telemachus the fair two-handled cup;
and in the same way the dear son of Odysseus prayed.
And when they had roasted the outer flesh and drawn it off,
they divided the portions and feasted a glorious feast.
But when they had put away the desire for drink and food,
then among them Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, began to speak:

Now it is fairer to inquire and to ask
70	the strangers who they are, since they have had their fill of food.
71	'Strangers, who are you? Whence do you sail the watery ways?
72	Is it on some business, or do you wander at random,
73	like pirates over the sea, who wander
74	staking their lives, bringing evil to men of other lands?'
75	Then wise Telemachus answered him in turn,
76	having taken courage; for Athena herself put courage in his heart,
77	that he might ask him about his absent father
78	and that he might have good fame among men:
79	O Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans,
you ask whence we are; and I will tell you.
We have come from Ithaca beneath Neion;
and this business is a private one, not public, which I speak of.
I am pursuing the wide fame of my father, if I may hear it anywhere,
of godlike, much-enduring Odysseus, who once, they say,
fighting beside you, sacked the city of the Trojans.
For of all the others, as many as fought against the Trojans,
we hear where each perished by a grievous death,
but of him the son of Cronos has made even the death unheard of.
For no one can say clearly where he has perished,
whether he was subdued on the mainland by hostile men,
or at sea among the waves of Amphitrite.
Therefore now I come to your knees, if you are willing
to tell of his grievous death, if somewhere you saw it
with your own eyes or heard the tale from another
wanderer; for his mother bore him beyond others to suffer.
And do not soften anything out of respect for me or pity,
but tell me well how you came to see it.
I beseech you, if ever my father, good Odysseus,
undertook and fulfilled for you any word or deed
in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes,
remember these things now for me, and tell me truly."
Then Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, answered him:

My friend, since you remind me of the misery which in that
104	land we endured, we sons of the Achaeans, of unrestrained might,
105	both all that we suffered with the ships on the misty sea
106	wandering after plunder, wherever Achilles led,
107	and all that around the great city of king Priam
108	we fought; and there then were slain all that were best.
109	There lies warlike Ajax, there Achilles,
110	there Patroclus, a counsellor equal to the gods,
111	there my dear son, at once strong and blameless,
112	Antilochus, exceeding swift of foot and a fighter;
113	and many other evils we suffered besides; who of mortal men
114	could tell all those things?
115	Not even if for five or six years you stayed on
116	and asked all the evils the noble Achaeans suffered there,
117	you would be weary and go back to your native land first.
118	For nine years we wove evils for them, working around them
119	with all kinds of tricks, and hardly did the son of Cronos bring it to an end.
120	There no one ever wished to be matched openly in counsel,
121	since godlike Odysseus far surpassed them
122	with all kinds of tricks, your father, if truly
123	you are his offspring; awe holds me as I look at you.
124	For indeed your words are like his, and you would not say
125	that a younger man could speak so like him.
126	There, as long as I and godlike Odysseus
127	never spoke apart, either in assembly or in council,
128	but with one heart, in mind and prudent counsel,
129	we planned for the Argives how things might be best.
130	But when we had sacked the steep city of Priam,
131	and went in the ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans,
132	even then Zeus was devising in his mind a grievous return
133	for the Argives, since not all of them were
134	sensible or just; therefore many of them met an evil fate
135	from the destructive wrath of the grey-eyed daughter of a mighty father.
136	She set strife between the two sons of Atreus.
137	And these two, having called an assembly of all the Achaeans,
138	recklessly, and not in due order, at sunset,
139	and the sons of the Achaeans came heavy with wine,
140	spoke their speech, for which they had gathered the people.
141	Then Menelaus bade all the Achaeans
142	think of their return over the broad back of the sea,
143	but to Agamemnon it was not pleasing at all; for he wished
144	to hold back the people and to offer sacred hecatombs,
145	so that he might appease the terrible wrath of Athena,
146	the fool, and he did not know this, that she was not going to be persuaded;
147	for the mind of the gods who are for ever is not quickly turned.
148	So these two stood, exchanging harsh words;
149	and the well-greaved Achaeans leapt up
150	with a marvellous din, and a divided counsel pleased them.
151	We passed the night, pondering grievous things in our hearts
152	against one another; for Zeus was devising the pain of evil.
153	At dawn some of us drew our ships to the divine sea
154	and put in our possessions and the deep-girdled women.
155	But half the people held back, remaining
156	there beside Agamemnon, son of Atreus, shepherd of the people;
157	and half of us embarked and rowed; and the ships very swiftly
158	sailed, and a god smoothed the sea full of monsters.
159	Coming to Tenedos we offered sacrifices to the gods,
160	longing for home; but Zeus did not yet plan our return,
161	cruel one, who raised evil strife a second time again.
162	Some turned their curved ships back and went
163	with lord Odysseus, shrewd of mind, of many wiles,
164	again bringing favour to Agamemnon, son of Atreus;
165	but I with the ships in a body, those that followed me,
166	fled, since I knew what evil the deity was devising.
167	And the warlike son of Tydeus fled, and urged on his companions.
168	And late after us came fair-haired Menelaus,
169	and found us on Lesbos pondering the long voyage,
170	whether we should sail above rugged Chios,
171	toward the isle of Psyria, keeping it on our left,
172	or below Chios, past windy Mimas.
173	We asked the god to show a sign; and he showed us,
174	and bade us cut across the open sea to Euboea,
175	so that we might escape most quickly from the evil.
176	And a shrill wind rose to blow; and the ships very swiftly
177	ran over the fishy paths, and to Geraestus
178	they came in by night; and to Poseidon many thigh-pieces
179	of bulls we laid, having measured the great sea.
180	It was the fourth day when at Argos the companions of Diomedes,
181	son of Tydeus, tamer of horses, set the balanced ships;
182	but I held on to Pylos, and never did the wind
183	fall, since the god first sent it forth to blow.
184	So I came, dear child, uninformed, and I know nothing
185	of those, which of the Achaeans were saved and which perished.
186	But whatever I learn sitting in our halls,
187	as is right, you shall learn, and I will not hide it from you.
188	They say the Myrmidons, famed for spears, came back well,
189	whom the glorious son of great-hearted Achilles led,
190	and well Philoctetes, the glorious son of Poias.
191	And Idomeneus brought all his companions to Crete,
192	who escaped from the war, and the sea took none of them away.
193	And of the son of Atreus you yourselves have heard, though far away,
194	how he came, and how Aegisthus devised a grievous death.
195	But indeed he paid terribly for it;
196	how good it is that a son should be left by a man who has died,
197	since he too took vengeance on his father's murderer,
198	Aegisthus of the crafty mind, who killed his famous father.
199	You too, my friend, for I see you handsome and tall,
200	be valiant, that even a later-born man may speak well of you.
Then wise Telemachus answered him in turn:

O Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans,
203	and indeed that man took vengeance, and the Achaeans
204	will carry his wide fame, for those to come to hear of it.
205	Would that the gods would put such power around me,
206	to take vengeance on the suitors for their grievous transgression,
207	who, insolent, devise reckless things against me.
208	But the gods have not spun for me such happiness,
209	for my father and for me; but now I must endure in any case.
Then Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, answered him:

My friend, since you have reminded me of this and spoken it,
212	they say that for the sake of your mother many suitors
213	in your halls, against your will, devise evils.
214	Tell me, do you submit willingly, or do the people
215	hate you throughout the district, following the voice of a god?
216	And who knows if he will not someday come and pay them back for their violence,
217	either alone, or all the Achaeans together?
218	For if grey-eyed Athena were willing to love you as
219	she then cared for glorious Odysseus
220	in the land of the Trojans, where we Achaeans suffered pains—
221	for I have never seen gods so openly loving,
222	as Pallas Athena stood openly beside him—
223	if she were willing to love you so and care for you in her heart,
224	then some of them would even forget about marriage.
Then wise Telemachus answered him in turn:
Then again the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, said to him:

Telemachus, what word has escaped the fence of your teeth!
231	Easily a god, if he wishes, can save a man even from afar.
232	I for my part would rather, after suffering many pains,
233	come home and see the day of return,
234	than come and perish at my own hearth, as Agamemnon
235	perished by the guile of Aegisthus and of his own wife.
236	But death, which is common to all, not even the gods
237	can ward off from a man dear to them, when once
238	the destructive fate of long-lasting death brings him down.
Then wise Telemachus answered her in turn:

Mentor, let us no longer speak of these things, though we care;
241	for him there is no longer a true return, but already
242	the immortals have contrived for him death and black doom.
243	But now I wish to enquire about another matter and to ask
244	Nestor, since he knows beyond others about justice and wisdom;
245	for they say he has ruled three generations of men;
246	so that he seems to me to look like an immortal.
247	O Nestor, son of Neleus, tell me the truth:
248	how did the son of Atreus, wide-ruling Agamemnon, die?
249	Where was Menelaus? What death did crafty-minded
250	Aegisthus devise for him, since he killed a man far better?
251	Was he not in Achaean Argos, but somewhere else
252	was wandering among men, and he took courage and killed him?
Then Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, answered him:

Therefore, child, I shall tell you all the truth.
255	Indeed you yourself imagine how it would have turned out,
256	if Aegisthus had been found alive in the halls
257	by the son of Atreus, fair-haired Menelaus, coming from Troy;
258	then they would not have heaped the piled earth over him even dead,
259	but dogs and birds would have torn him
260	as he lay in the plain far from the city, and no one
261	of the Achaean women would have wept for him; for he had devised a very great deed.
262	For we there were completing many labours
263	and sat; but he, at ease in a recess of horse-nurturing Argos,
264	kept beguiling Agamemnon's wife with many words.
265	And she, at first, refused the unseemly deed,
266	godlike Clytaemnestra; for she had good sense in her mind;
267	and beside her was also a singer, to whom much
268	the son of Atreus, going to Troy, had charged to guard his wife.
269	But when the fate of the gods bound her to be subdued,
270	then he took the singer to a desert island
271	and left him to become prey and spoil for birds,
272	and her, willing, he led willingly to his own house.
273	And many thigh-pieces he burned on the sacred altars of the gods,
274	and many offerings he hung up, textiles and gold,
275	having accomplished a great deed, which he never expected in his heart.
276	For we together were sailing, coming from Troy,
277	the son of Atreus and I, being friends with one another;
278	but when we reached holy Sunium, the cape of Athens,
279	there Phoebus Apollo, coming upon the helmsman of Menelaus
280	with his gentle shafts, killed him,
281	holding the steering-oar in his hands, as the ship ran on,
282	Phrontis, son of Onetor, who excelled the tribes of men
283	in steering a ship, whenever the storm-winds rushed.
284	So he was held back there, though eager for the journey,
285	until he might bury his companion and perform the funeral rites.
286	But when he too, going over the wine-dark sea
287	in the hollow ships, reached the steep mountain of Malea
288	running, then wide-seeing Zeus devised a hateful journey,
289	and poured out the blast of shrill winds,
290	and the waves swelled monstrous, equal to mountains.
291	There, splitting up the ships, he brought some to Crete,
292	where the Cydonians lived around the streams of the Iardanus.
293	There is a certain smooth and sheer rock running into the sea
294	at the edge of Gortyn in the misty sea;
295	there the South Wind drives a great wave against the left headland,
296	toward Phaestus, and a small stone holds back a great wave.
297	Some came there, and with effort the men escaped destruction,
298	but the waves broke the ships against the reefs;
299	and the five dark-prowed ships
300	wind and water carried and brought near to Egypt.
301	So he there, gathering much livelihood and gold,
302	wandered with his ships among men of other tongues;
303	and meanwhile Aegisthus devised these grievous things at home.
305	And for seven years he ruled Mycenae rich in gold,
304	having killed the son of Atreus, and the people were subdued under him.
306	But in the eighth year, to his evil, godlike Orestes came
307	back from Athens, and killed his father's murderer,
308	Aegisthus of the crafty mind, who had killed his famous father.
309	Indeed, having killed him, he gave the Argives a funeral feast
310	for his hateful mother and for cowardly Aegisthus;
311	and on that same day came to him Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
312	bringing many possessions, as many as his ships bore as burden.
313	And you, friend, do not wander long far from your home,
314	leaving behind your possessions and men in your house
315	so overbearing, lest they eat up all your
316	possessions, dividing them, and you go on a fruitless journey.
317	But to Menelaus I urge and bid you
318	to go; for he has newly come from elsewhere,
319	from among the people from whence one would not hope in one's heart
320	to come, whomever storms first drive astray
321	into such a great sea, from which not even birds
322	fly in the same year, so great and terrible it is.
323	But go now with your ship and your companions;
324	or if you wish to go by land, a chariot and horses are here for you,
325	and here are my sons, who will be your escorts
326	to divine Lacedaemon, where fair-haired Menelaus is.
327	And beseech him yourself, that he may speak unerringly;
328	and a lie he will not tell, for he is very wise.
So he spoke, and the sun set and darkness came on.
And among them spoke the goddess, grey-eyed Athena:

Old man, indeed you have told these things according to what is right.
332	But come, cut out the tongues, and mix the wine,
333	so that, having poured libations to Poseidon and the other immortals,
334	we may think of bed; for it is the time for it.
335	For already the light has gone under the gloom, and it is not fitting
336	to sit long at the feast of the gods, but to go.
So spoke the daughter of Zeus, and they heard her as she spoke.
For them the heralds poured water on their hands,
and the youths filled the mixing-bowls with drink,
and distributed it to all, having first poured drops in the cups;
and they threw the tongues in the fire, and standing poured libations.
But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their heart wished,
then Athena and godlike Telemachus
both set out to go to the hollow ship.
But Nestor held them back, addressing them with words:

May Zeus ward that off, and the other immortal gods,
347	that you should go from me to the swift ship
348	as from someone quite without clothing and poor,
349	who has not many cloaks and blankets in his house,
350	nor for himself nor for guests to sleep softly.
351	But I have cloaks and fine blankets.
352	Surely never will the dear son of this man Odysseus
353	lie down on the deck of a ship, while I
354	am alive, and afterwards sons are left in my halls,
355	to entertain guests, whoever comes to my house.
Then again the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, said to him:

You have spoken well in this, dear old man; and it is fitting for you
358	that Telemachus obey, since it is much better so.
359	So this man will now follow you, that he may sleep
360	in your halls; but I will go to the black ship,
361	to encourage my companions and tell each thing.
362	For I alone among them claim to be the older;
363	the others follow in friendship, younger men,
364	all of the age of great-hearted Telemachus.
365	There I would lie down by the hollow black ship
366	now; but at dawn I shall go to the great-hearted Caucones,
367	where a debt is owed to me, by no means new
368	nor small. But you, since this man has come to your house,
369	send him with a chariot and your son; and give him horses,
370	those that are lightest to run and best in strength.
So speaking, grey-eyed Athena departed
likened to a sea-eagle; and amazement took all who saw.
And the old man marvelled, when he saw with his eyes;
and he took the hand of Telemachus, and spoke a word and called him by name:

My friend, I do not expect that you will be bad and without valour,
376	if indeed, young as you are, gods follow you as escorts thus.
377	For this was no other of those who hold Olympian houses,
378	but the daughter of Zeus, most glorious Tritogeneia,
379	who also honoured your noble father among the Argives.
380	But, lady, be gracious, and give me good fame,
381	to myself and my children and my revered wife;
382	and to you I will sacrifice a broad-browed yearling heifer,
383	untamed, which no man has yet led under the yoke;
384	her I will sacrifice to you, pouring gold about her horns.
So he spoke praying, and Pallas Athena heard him.
And Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, led them,
his sons and sons-in-law, to his fair house.
But when they came to the far-famed house of that lord,
they sat in order on the chairs and high seats;
and for them as they came the old man mixed a bowl
of sweet-drinking wine, which in the eleventh year
the housekeeper opened, and loosed the stopper from it;
of this the old man mixed a bowl, and he prayed much
to Athena, pouring libations, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus.
But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their heart wished,
they went each to his own house to lie down,
and there Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, put to bed
Telemachus, dear son of godlike Odysseus,
on a bedstead of rope-strung frame under the echoing portico,
and beside him Peisistratus of the good ash-spear, leader of men,
who was still unmarried among the sons in the halls;
and he himself slept in the inner part of the lofty house,
and for him his wife, the lady, prepared bed and couch.
When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, rose from his bed,
and going out sat down on the polished stones,
which were before the lofty doors,
white, gleaming with oil; on which before
Neleus used to sit, a counsellor equal to the gods;
but he, subdued by fate, had already gone to Hades,
and Nestor the Gerenian then sat there, guardian of the Achaeans,
holding a sceptre. And around him his sons gathered in a throng
coming from their chambers, Echephron and Stratius
and Perseus and Aretus and godlike Thrasymedes.
And after them the sixth, the hero Peisistratus, came,
and they led godlike Telemachus and seated him beside.
And among them Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, began to speak:

Quickly, dear children, accomplish my wish for me,
419	that first of the gods I may propitiate Athena,
420	who came to me manifestly to the rich feast of the god.
421	But come, let one go to the plain for a heifer, that as quickly as possible
422	she may come, and let a cattle-herding man drive her;
423	and let one go to the black ship of great-hearted Telemachus
424	and bring all the companions, and leave only two;
425	and let another bid the goldsmith Laerces come
426	here, that he may pour gold about the horns of the heifer.
427	And you others stay here all together, and tell the maids inside
428	to prepare a feast throughout the far-famed house,
429	and to bring seats and wood about and bright water.
So he spoke, and they all were busy. The heifer came
from the plain, and there came from the swift balanced ship
the companions of great-hearted Telemachus, and the smith came
holding in his hands the bronze tools, the implements of his craft,
an anvil and a hammer and well-made tongs,
with which he worked gold; and Athena came
to meet the sacrifices. And the old man Nestor, driver of horses,
gave gold; and he then poured it about the horns of the heifer,
working it skilfully, that the goddess might rejoice at the offering when she saw it.
Stratius and godlike Echephron led the heifer by the horns.
And Aretus came from the chamber bringing for them lustral water
in a flowered basin, and in the other hand he held barley-grains
in a basket; and Thrasymedes, steadfast in battle,
stood by holding a sharp axe in his hand, to strike the heifer.
Perseus held the bowl for the blood; and the old man Nestor, driver of horses,
began with the water and barley-grains, and prayed much to Athena,
beginning the offering, throwing hairs from the head in the fire.
But when they had prayed and scattered the barley-grains,
at once Nestor's son, high-spirited Thrasymedes,
struck, standing near; and the axe cut through the tendons
of the neck, and loosed the strength of the heifer. And they cried out,
the daughters and the daughters-in-law and the revered wife
of Nestor, Eurydice, eldest of the daughters of Clymenus.
Then they lifted her up from the broad-wayed earth
and held her; and Peisistratus, leader of men, cut her throat.
And when the dark blood flowed from her, and the spirit left the bones,
quickly they cut her up, and at once cut out the thigh-pieces
all in due order, and covered them with fat,
making them double, and laid raw pieces on them.
And the old man burned them on split wood, and poured sparkling wine
over them; and young men beside him held five-pronged forks in their hands.
But when the thigh-pieces were burned and they had tasted the innards,
they cut up the rest and pierced it on spits,
and roasted it holding the pointed spits in their hands.
Meanwhile fair Polycaste bathed Telemachus,
the youngest daughter of Nestor, son of Neleus.
But when she had bathed him and anointed him with rich oil,
and had cast about him a fair cloak and a tunic,
he came out of the bath looking like the immortals;
and going he sat down beside Nestor, shepherd of the people.
And when they had roasted the outer flesh and drawn it off,
they sat and feasted; and good men rose
pouring wine in golden cups.
But when they had put away the desire for drink and food,
among them Nestor, the Gerenian horseman, began to speak:

My sons, come, for Telemachus yoke the fair-maned horses
476	under the chariot, bringing them, that he may make his journey.
So he spoke, and they heard him well and obeyed,
and quickly yoked the swift horses under the chariot.
And the housekeeper put in bread and wine
and meats, such as Zeus-nurtured kings eat.
And Telemachus mounted the very beautiful chariot;
and beside him Nestor's son Peisistratus, leader of men,
mounted the chariot and took the reins in his hands,
and lashed to drive, and the two horses flew not unwilling
to the plain, and left the steep citadel of Pylos.
And all day long they shook the yoke they held on both sides.
And the sun set and all the ways were shadowed,
and they came to Pherae, to the house of Diocles,
son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheus begot as a son.
There they passed the night, and he set guest-gifts beside them.
When early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
they yoked the horses and mounted the intricate chariot;
and drove out from the forecourt and the echoing portico;
and he lashed to drive, and the two horses flew not unwilling.
And they came to the wheat-bearing plain, and there then
they finished their journey; so well did the swift horses carry them.
And the sun set and all the ways were shadowed.
